title: Antiferromagnetism
short_inter: Antiferromagnetism is a magnetic phenomenon in which adjacent atomic magnetic moments spontaneously align in opposite directions, resulting in zero net macroscopic magnetization below a characteristic temperature known as the Néel temperature. Above this temperature, the material transitions to a paramagnetic state.
short_intro: Antiferromagnetism is a magnetic phenomenon in which adjacent atomic magnetic moments spontaneously align in opposite directions, resulting in zero net macroscopic magnetization below a characteristic temperature known as the Néel temperature. Above this temperature, the material transitions to a paramagnetic state.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of atomic magnetic dipole alignment, definition of Néel temperature, comparison with ferromagnetism and paramagnetism, and the behavior of magnetic susceptibility above the Néel temperature (Curie-Weiss law modification).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative treatment using molecular field theory, derivation of magnetic susceptibility below and above the Néel temperature, sub-lattice magnetization behavior, and temperature dependence of susceptibility.

prerequisites: Origin of magnetic moments in atoms and Hund's rules
Curie-Weiss law in paramagnetism and ferromagnetism

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Origin of Antiferromagnetism
bullets: Adjacent magnetic moments are coupled via an exchange interaction that favors antiparallel alignment due to the overlap of electronic wavefunctions.
The exchange integral (J) is negative, distinguishing it from ferromagnetism where J is positive.
The crystal lattice can be visualized as two interpenetrating sub-lattices (A and B) with opposite magnetization vectors (M<sub>A</sub> and M<sub>B</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Temperature Dependence and Néel Temperature (T<sub>N</sub>)
bullets: Below the Néel temperature (T<sub>N</sub>), thermal agitation is insufficient to disrupt the antiparallel ordering, yielding zero net magnetization in the absence of an external field.
As temperature increases toward T<sub>N</sub>, the sub-lattice magnetizations decrease gradually to zero.
For T > T<sub>N</sub>, the thermal energy completely overcomes the short-range exchange forces, and the material exhibits paramagnetic behavior.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Susceptibility Behavior
bullets: Unlike ferromagnets whose susceptibility follows the Curie-Weiss law with a positive paramagnetic Curie temperature, antiferromagnets exhibit a susceptibility that decreases with decreasing temperature below T<sub>N</sub>.
At T = T<sub>N</sub>, the magnetic susceptibility reaches a sharp maximum.
Above T<sub>N</sub>, the susceptibility follows the modified Curie-Weiss law: χ = C / (T + θ), where θ is the paramagnetic Curie temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Other Magnetic Materials
bullets: Antiferromagnetic materials have zero spontaneous macroscopic magnetization, unlike ferromagnets and ferrimagnets.
Examples of antiferromagnetic materials include Manganese oxide (MnO), Nickel oxide (NiO), and Chromium (Cr).
They show no magnetic hysteresis loops under normal conditions because domain walls do not contribute to net moments without an applied asymmetric field.

derivations.title: Molecular Field Theory for Antiferromagnetic Susceptibility (T > T_N)
derivations.conditions: Temperature T greater than the Néel temperature T_N, two-sublattice model
steps: Consider two interpenetrating sub-lattices A and B with magnetizations M<sub>A</sub> and M<sub>B</sub> under an applied magnetic field B.
The effective magnetic field acting on sub-lattice A is given by B<sub>eff,A</sub> = B - λ M<sub>B</sub>, where λ is the molecular field coefficient (λ > 0).
Similarly, for sub-lattice B, B<sub>eff,B</sub> = B - λ M<sub>A</sub>.

Using the Curie law for each sub-lattice in the paramagnetic region, M<sub>A</sub> = [C / (2T)] (B - λ M<sub>B</sub>) and M<sub>B</sub> = [C / (2T)] (B - λ M<sub>A</sub>), where C is the Curie constant for the whole system.
Adding and solving these simultaneous equations for total magnetization M = M<sub>A</sub> + M<sub>B</sub> yields the susceptibility χ = M / B = C / (T + λC).

derivations.title: Susceptibility at Absolute Zero (T = 0 K) for Parallel Field
derivations.conditions: Applied field parallel to the easy axis of antiferromagnetic alignment at T = 0 K
steps: At T = 0 K, sub-lattice magnetizations are fully saturated at M<sub>0</sub>.
When a weak magnetic field B is applied parallel to the alignment axis, it tilts both sub-lattice vectors slightly by an angle θ toward the field direction.
The component of magnetization along the field is M = 2 M<sub>0</sub> sin(θ).
The torque balance per sub-lattice equates the external magnetic torque (M<sub>0</sub> B cos(θ)) to the molecular field restoring torque (λ M<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> sin(θ)).
Solving for sin(θ) in the small angle limit gives sin(θ) = B / (λ M<sub>0</sub>), leading to M = 2 M<sub>0</sub> B / (λ M<sub>0</sub>) = 2 B / λ.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Susceptibility vs Temperature (χ-T) Curve for Antiferromagnetic Material
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing susceptibility increasing linearly with temperature in the paramagnetic region (T > T_N), reaching a sharp cusp or maximum at T = T_N, and then decreasing as T approaches 0 K.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The sharp peak marks the Néel temperature where antiparallel ordering sets in. Below T_N, thermal fluctuations alter the alignment differently depending on field orientation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in multiple-choice questions to identify the characteristic susceptibility graph of antiferromagnetic substances compared to ferromagnetic and paramagnetic graphs.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Sub-lattice Magnetization vs Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot starting at maximum value M<sub>0</sub> at T = 0 K, curving downwards smoothly with increasing temperature, and dropping sharply to zero exactly at T = T_N.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the thermal disordering of individual sub-lattice alignment vectors, mirroring Brillouin function behavior in ferromagnets.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test understanding of order-disorder phase transitions in magnetic lattices.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Neutron Diffraction Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of a neutron beam incident on an antiferromagnetic powder sample, producing distinct magnetic Bragg peaks in addition to nuclear scattering peaks.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Because neutrons possess a magnetic moment and a wavelength comparable to interatomic spacing, they can probe the alternating magnetic unit cell, which has a lattice parameter twice that of the chemical unit cell.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in PGT examinations as the primary experimental proof verifying antiferromagnetic atomic ordering.

solved_numericals.question: An antiferromagnetic material has a paramagnetic Curie temperature θ = 60 K and a Néel temperature T_N = 50 K. Calculate the ratio θ / T_N and state if this is typical.
solution_steps: Identify given values: θ = 60 K, T_N = 50 K.
Conclusion: In many real antiferromagnetic crystals, θ is roughly equal to or slightly greater than T_N due to next-nearest-neighbor interactions.

solved_numericals.question: The magnetic susceptibility of an antiferromagnetic material above its Néel temperature is given by χ = C / (T + θ). If C = 1.5 K and θ = 30 K, calculate the susceptibility at T = 70 K.
solution_steps: Substitute the given values: C = 1.5 K, T = 70 K, θ = 30 K.

solved_numericals.question: Using the molecular field approximation, if the molecular field constant λ for an antiferromagnetic solid is 500 mol/m<sup>3</sup>, determine the perpendicular susceptibility χ<sub>⊥</sub> at T = 0 K.
solution_steps: Recall the relation for perpendicular susceptibility at T = 0 K: χ<sub>⊥</sub> = 1 / λ.

Substitute λ = 500 mol/m<sup>3</sup> (assuming standard SI volume normalization, or unitless convention where λ is dimensionless volumetric parameter; here use standard dimensionless SI susceptibility relations where χ<sub>⊥</sub> = 1 / λ).

assumptions_and_limitations: The molecular field theory assumes a uniform average magnetic field acting on each sub-lattice, which neglects local spatial fluctuations of spins.
It assumes localized magnetic moments (Heisenberg model with fixed localized spins), which fails for itinerant (band) antiferromagnets like chromium.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Antiferromagnetic materials have permanent net macroscopic magnetization.
common_misconceptions.correct: Antiferromagnetic materials have zero net macroscopic magnetization below the Néel temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: The opposing magnetic moments of adjacent atoms cancel each other out completely.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Susceptibility increases continuously with temperature in antiferromagnets.
common_misconceptions.correct: Susceptibility increases with temperature only below the Néel temperature; above it, susceptibility decreases according to the Curie-Weiss law.
common_misconceptions.why: The Néel temperature represents a critical transition point where thermal energy begins to dominate over exchange coupling.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Antiferromagnetism exhibits strong magnetic hysteresis like ferromagnetism.
common_misconceptions.correct: Antiferromagnets show practically linear field dependence and no remanent magnetization or coercivity.
common_misconceptions.why: The absence of net moment prevents typical ferromagnetic domain wall pinning hysteresis effects.

quick_revision: Antiferromagnetism is characterized by antiparallel alignment of adjacent atomic magnetic moments and zero net magnetization.
The transition temperature is called the Néel temperature (T_N).
Magnetic susceptibility reaches a maximum at T = T_N and follows χ = C / (T + θ) for T > T_N.
